triage.name: Ovarian Cysts
triage.reason: Common cause of pelvic pain or incidental adnexal mass; reachable by history, exam and pelvic ultrasound with clear differential including torsion.

demographics: Most common in women of reproductive age, especially during the years of regular ovulation
Functional cysts are uncommon before menarche and become less frequent after menopause
Incidental cysts are frequently found on pelvic imaging done for other reasons

risk_factors.text: Reproductive age with regular ovulatory cycles
Current or prior use of fertility medications that induce ovulation
Prior pelvic infection or pelvic surgery

chief_complaints.text: I have a dull ache low down on one side of my belly
I feel bloated and full in my lower belly
My doctor found a cyst on an ultrasound and I'm worried about it

hpi.onset: Often gradual and vague; may be discovered incidentally on imaging done for another reason
hpi.duration: Days to weeks of mild symptoms, or an incidental finding of unknown duration
hpi.progression: Usually stable or slowly improving; a functional cyst often shrinks over one to three cycles
hpi.location: Lower abdomen or pelvis, typically on one side
hpi.radiation: May radiate to the lower back, upper thigh or groin on the same side
hpi.quality: Dull, pressure-like or achy; can become sharp and severe if the cyst ruptures or twists
hpi.severity: Mild to moderate, 3–5/10; severe if rupture or torsion occurs
hpi.timing: Intermittent, often worse around the middle or second half of the menstrual cycle

associated_symptoms.text: Urinary frequency or urgency from pressure on the bladder

pertinent_negatives: Vaginal bleeding between periods or after intercourse
Severe constant pain with vomiting and fainting
Early satiety or increasing abdominal girth over weeks

atypical.how_it_differs: Functional cysts are uncommon before menarche; when present they are usually incidental or cause vague abdominal pain rather than a clear cyclic pattern.
After menopause, cysts are more often asymptomatic and found incidentally, but the risk of malignancy is higher, so any new cyst needs evaluation.
Cysts are often found on routine obstetric ultrasound; most are simple and resolve, but larger ones can cause pain or, rarely, torsion.
Pelvic pain may be less well localized and the cyst may be harder to palpate on exam, so imaging is more often needed.

general.mild: Comfortable, no distress; normal general appearance
general.moderate: Mild discomfort, shifts position occasionally, otherwise well-appearing
general.severe: Ill-appearing, guarding the lower abdomen, reluctant to move
general.critical: Toxic-appearing, pale, diaphoretic, tachycardic, may be hypotensive if a cyst has ruptured with bleeding

findings.maneuver: Palpate all four quadrants, starting away from the area of pain
findings.finding: Unilateral lower abdominal tenderness on the side of the cyst

findings.maneuver: Perform a bimanual pelvic exam with one hand on the abdomen and two fingers in the vagina
findings.finding: Palpable adnexal mass or fullness on one side, separate from the uterus

findings.maneuver: Palpate the adnexa during bimanual exam
findings.finding: Focal tenderness over the adnexa on the affected side

findings.maneuver: Move the cervix side to side during the pelvic exam
Assess uterine size and shape during bimanual exam
Palpate the abdomen and observe for involuntary guarding
Assess for rebound tenderness or ask the patient to cough
Auscultate bowel sounds in all four quadrants

findings.finding: Normal external genitalia without lesions, discharge or erythema

findings.maneuver: Palpate the inguinal and supraclavicular lymph nodes

labs.caveat: Must be negative. A positive result redirects the workup to pregnancy-related causes such as ectopic pregnancy or a corpus luteum cyst of pregnancy.
Low only when a cyst has ruptured and bled significantly; a normal value does not exclude slow bleeding.
Mild elevation is nonspecific; marked elevation points toward infection such as a tubo-ovarian abscess rather than an uncomplicated cyst.
Nonspecific; helps support an inflammatory or infectious alternative when the presentation is atypical.
Mild sterile pyuria can occur from irritation of the bladder by a large cyst and may falsely suggest a urinary tract infection.
Microscopic hematuria is nonspecific and can also reflect a urinary stone or infection.
Hypothyroidism is a weak risk factor for cyst formation and can also cause menstrual irregularity that mimics cyst-related symptoms.

imaging.study: Pelvic ultrasound (transvaginal, with transabdominal views as needed)
imaging.preferred_when: First-line imaging in all patients; transvaginal gives the best resolution in sexually active or adult patients

findings.text: Simple cyst: thin smooth wall, anechoic fluid, no internal septations, no solid components, no internal flow
Unilateral adnexal cyst separate from the ovary or arising from it
Normal ovarian parenchyma and normal uterus
Hemorrhagic cyst: internal echoes or a reticular lacy pattern with no internal flow
Complex features: thick wall, septations, solid components or papillary projections
Free pelvic fluid, which may be simple or echogenic if a cyst has ruptured and bled
Enlarged ovary with peripherally displaced follicles and a twisted vascular pedicle (ovarian torsion)
Absent or markedly reduced Doppler flow within the affected ovary (ovarian torsion)

imaging.study: Color and spectral Doppler of the ovaries and adnexa
imaging.preferred_when: Added whenever torsion is suspected or a mass has solid or vascular components

findings.text: Normal arterial and venous flow in the affected ovary, which does not fully exclude torsion
Absent or reduced diastolic flow with an elevated resistive index in the affected ovary
No internal vascularity within a simple or hemorrhagic cyst
Internal vascularity within solid components of a complex mass

imaging.study: MRI pelvis with and without IV contrast
imaging.preferred_when: Indeterminate adnexal mass on ultrasound, or when ultrasound is technically limited

findings.text: Characterizes a cyst as simple, hemorrhagic or complex when ultrasound is equivocal
Hemorrhagic cyst: high signal on T1 with shading on T2 and no enhancement
Solid enhancing components or thick irregular septations suggesting a neoplasm

imaging.study: CT abdomen and pelvis with IV contrast
imaging.preferred_when: Not for routine cyst evaluation; used when another acute abdominal process is suspected or ultrasound is unavailable in an unstable patient

findings.text: Incidental simple adnexal cyst with water-density contents and a thin wall
Complex or solid adnexal mass with enhancement
Hemoperitoneum or active contrast extravasation from a ruptured cyst
Ovarian enlargement with surrounding fat stranding and a twisted pedicle (torsion)
No role in evaluating an ovarian cyst; may show nonspecific bowel gas or a calcification but does not characterize adnexal masses

initial.why: Rules out pregnancy and ectopic pregnancy before any imaging or intervention in anyone who could be pregnant

initial.test: Pelvic ultrasound (transvaginal, with transabdominal views as needed)
initial.why: First-line study to confirm the cyst, define its size and morphology, and assess for torsion or rupture
Baseline blood count; a low hemoglobin or hematocrit raises concern for a ruptured hemorrhagic cyst
initial.only_if: Baseline blood count; a low hemoglobin or hematocrit raises concern for a ruptured hemorrhagic cyst

initial.why: Screens for urinary tract infection or stone, common mimics of pelvic pain

initial.test: Color and spectral Doppler of the ovaries and adnexa
initial.only_if: ovarian torsion is suspected (severe pain, nausea, adnexal tenderness)

supporting.why: Supports an infectious or inflammatory alternative when fever or marked tenderness is present
Nonspecific inflammatory marker that can support an alternative diagnosis
Raises concern for malignancy in a complex or suspicious mass
supporting.only_if: postmenopausal woman or imaging shows a complex/solid adnexal mass

supporting.why: Evaluates thyroid dysfunction as a contributor to menstrual irregularity
supporting.only_if: irregular menses or other features suggest thyroid disease

supporting.test: MRI pelvis with and without IV contrast
supporting.why: Characterizes an adnexal mass that remains indeterminate on ultrasound
supporting.only_if: ultrasound is equivocal or technically limited

not_indicated.test: CT abdomen and pelvis with IV contrast
not_indicated.why: Not needed for a typical simple cyst; exposes the patient to radiation and is less specific than ultrasound
Does not characterize adnexal masses and rarely changes management
Not a screening test for benign cysts in premenopausal women; can be falsely elevated by endometriosis, fibroids or pregnancy
No role in the evaluation of pelvic pain or an adnexal mass
Not needed unless the pain is epigastric and pancreatitis is suspected
Not routinely needed for an asymptomatic incidental simple cyst found on imaging

decision_points: Pregnancy test before imaging or intervention in anyone who could be pregnant
Transvaginal ultrasound is first-line; add Doppler when torsion is suspected
Simple cysts under about 5 cm in a premenopausal woman can be followed without intervention
Complex, solid or enlarging masses, or any cyst in a postmenopausal woman, need gynecology referral and possible surgical evaluation
Severe pain with nausea, vomiting or syncope raises concern for torsion or rupture and requires urgent evaluation

differential.name: Ovarian torsion
differential.why_considered: Sudden severe one-sided pelvic pain with nausea and vomiting, often in a patient with a known cyst
differential.trigger: Abrupt onset of severe unilateral pelvic pain with vomiting, especially with a known cyst larger than 5 cm

history: Sudden, severe, constant pain that builds over minutes to hours
Vomiting at or near the onset of pain
Known ovarian cyst or prior episodes of similar pain that resolved
exam: Ill-appearing, reluctant to move, may have low-grade fever
labs: Nonspecific; mild leukocytosis may be present
imaging: Enlarged, edematous ovary with peripherally displaced follicles
Absent or markedly reduced Doppler flow within the affected ovary

differential.name: Ectopic pregnancy
differential.why_considered: Unilateral pelvic pain in a patient of reproductive age who could be pregnant
differential.trigger: Any patient of reproductive age with pelvic pain until a pregnancy test is negative

history: Missed or abnormal period
Vaginal spotting or bleeding
Prior ectopic pregnancy, pelvic infection or tubal surgery
exam: Signs of peritoneal irritation or hemodynamic instability if ruptured
labs: Low or suboptimally rising hCG for gestational age
imaging: No intrauterine pregnancy on transvaginal ultrasound
Adnexal mass or gestational sac with or without fetal cardiac activity

differential.name: Pelvic inflammatory disease
differential.why_considered: Lower abdominal and pelvic pain with discharge or fever in a sexually active patient
differential.trigger: Fever, purulent vaginal discharge, or cervical motion tenderness

history: Bilateral rather than one-sided pain
New or multiple sexual partners, or a partner with symptoms
Vaginal discharge, abnormal bleeding, dyspareunia
exam: Uterine or adnexal tenderness, often bilateral
labs: Positive nucleic acid testing for chlamydia or gonorrhea

differential.name: Ruptured ovarian cyst
differential.why_considered: Sudden severe one-sided pelvic pain in a patient with a known or suspected cyst
differential.trigger: Sudden sharp pain with a drop in blood pressure or heart rate elevation after a known cyst

history: Sudden sharp pain, often during exercise or intercourse
Pain may improve after the initial tear, then worsen if bleeding continues
Known cyst or recent imaging showing a cyst
exam: Focal lower abdominal and adnexal tenderness
Tachycardia or hypotension if bleeding is heavy
labs: Positive pregnancy test excludes this diagnosis
imaging: Free pelvic fluid, often echogenic if hemoperitoneum
Active contrast extravasation on CT if bleeding is ongoing

differential.name: Appendicitis
differential.why_considered: Right lower quadrant pain with nausea in a patient with an adnexal cyst

history: Periumbilical pain migrating to the right lower quadrant
Anorexia, nausea, vomiting
Pain worsened by movement or cough
exam: Right lower quadrant tenderness with rebound or guarding
imaging: Enlarged non-compressible appendix with surrounding fat stranding

differential.name: Urinary tract infection
differential.why_considered: Pelvic pressure, urinary frequency and urgency that can mimic cyst-related symptoms

history: Dysuria, urgency, frequency
Suprapubic discomfort
No cyclic or positional component
exam: No adnexal mass or focal adnexal tenderness
labs: Positive leukocyte esterase and nitrites on urinalysis
imaging: Not routinely indicated; ultrasound may show a normal adnexa and no cyst

differential.name: Nephrolithiasis
differential.why_considered: One-sided flank or lower abdominal pain with nausea

history: Colicky pain radiating from flank to groin
Patient writhes and cannot get comfortable
Prior stone history
exam: No adnexal mass or focal adnexal tenderness
imaging: Stone in the ureter or kidney with hydronephrosis on CT

differential.name: Endometriosis
differential.why_considered: Chronic cyclic pelvic pain and dyspareunia that can be confused with cyst-related pain

history: Chronic pelvic pain worse with menses
Deep dyspareunia
Dyschezia or painful defecation during menses
Infertility
exam: Tender nodularity in the posterior cul-de-sac or uterosacral ligaments
Adnexal tenderness or mass from endometrioma
labs: CA-125 may be mildly elevated but is nonspecific
imaging: Endometrioma: homogeneous low-level internal echoes ('ground glass') without internal flow

differential.name: Ovarian cancer
differential.why_considered: Adnexal mass, especially in a postmenopausal woman or with persistent bloating and early satiety
differential.trigger: Postmenopausal woman with a new adnexal cyst, or any woman with persistent bloating, early satiety, weight loss or a complex mass

history: Persistent bloating, early satiety, increasing abdominal girth
Unintentional weight loss
Postmenopausal bleeding or new pelvic pain
Family history of breast or ovarian cancer
labs: Ascitic fluid may contain malignant cells
imaging: Complex cyst with thick irregular walls, septations, solid components or papillary projections
Ascites, omental caking or peritoneal implants

severity.mild: Small simple cyst, often asymptomatic or mild dull one-sided pelvic pressure; no fever, no peritoneal signs, normal vitals
severity.moderate: Larger or symptomatic cyst with moderate pelvic pain, bloating, or pain with intercourse; may have mild adnexal tenderness but remains well-appearing
severity.severe: Cyst causing severe pain, or complicated by rupture with significant bleeding or by torsion; ill-appearing, tachycardic, may have peritoneal signs
severity.critical: Ruptured cyst with hemodynamic instability from hemoperitoneum, or torsion with ovarian infarction and sepsis; hypotensive, pale, diaphoretic

red_flags.finding: Sudden severe unilateral pelvic pain with vomiting
red_flags.meaning: Ovarian torsion until proven otherwise; needs urgent surgical evaluation
Ruptured cyst with significant hemoperitoneum or another cause of intra-abdominal bleeding
Rupture with peritoneal irritation or another acute abdominal process

red_flags.finding: Fever with pelvic pain and purulent discharge
red_flags.meaning: Pelvic inflammatory disease or tubo-ovarian abscess
Ectopic pregnancy or pregnancy-related cyst; redirects the workup

red_flags.finding: Postmenopausal woman with a new complex or solid adnexal mass
red_flags.meaning: Malignancy until proven otherwise; needs gynecologic oncology referral

complications.name: Rupture with hemoperitoneum
clues: Free echogenic pelvic fluid on ultrasound

complications.name: Hemorrhagic cyst
clues: Internal echoes or lacy pattern on ultrasound
No internal flow within the cyst

complications.name: Malignant transformation
clues: Complex or solid mass with septations or papillary projections
Persistent bloating, early satiety, weight loss

special_populations.differences: Functional cysts are uncommon before menarche; when present they are usually incidental or cause vague abdominal pain. Torsion risk is higher because of the longer utero-ovarian ligament, so sudden severe pain warrants urgent ultrasound.

After menopause, cysts are more often asymptomatic and found incidentally, but the risk of malignancy is higher. Any new cyst in a postmenopausal woman needs evaluation with ultrasound and CA-125, and referral to gynecology.

Cysts are often found on routine obstetric ultrasound. Most are simple and resolve, but larger ones can cause pain or, rarely, torsion. Management must consider fetal safety; MRI without gadolinium may be used if ultrasound is equivocal.

Pelvic pain may be less well localized and the cyst may be harder to palpate on exam, so imaging is more often needed. Transvaginal ultrasound may be technically limited; transabdominal views or MRI may be required.

key_questions.question: Where is the pain, and is it on one side or both?
key_questions.looking_for: Unilateral lower abdominal or pelvic pain on the side of the cyst; bilateral pain suggests pelvic inflammatory disease or another cause

key_questions.question: When did the pain start, and was the onset sudden or gradual?
key_questions.looking_for: Gradual, vague onset favors an uncomplicated cyst; sudden severe onset raises concern for rupture or torsion

key_questions.question: How severe is the pain, and does it come and go or stay constant?
key_questions.looking_for: Mild to moderate intermittent pain typical of a simple cyst; severe constant pain suggests a complication

key_questions.question: Does the pain get worse with activity, intercourse, or sudden movements?
key_questions.looking_for: Worse with movement, exercise or intercourse from pressure or peritoneal irritation

key_questions.question: Have you had nausea or vomiting, especially right when the pain started?
key_questions.looking_for: Vomiting at the onset of severe pain suggests ovarian torsion

key_questions.question: Have you felt bloated, full, or noticed increasing abdominal girth?
key_questions.looking_for: Bloating and fullness are common with cysts; persistent bloating with early satiety or weight loss raises concern for malignancy

key_questions.question: Have you had any fever or chills?
key_questions.looking_for: Fever suggests infection such as pelvic inflammatory disease or tubo-ovarian abscess rather than an uncomplicated cyst

key_questions.question: When was your last menstrual period, and could you be pregnant?
key_questions.looking_for: A missed period or possible pregnancy redirects the workup to ectopic pregnancy or a pregnancy-related cyst

key_questions.question: Have your periods been regular, and have you had any bleeding between periods or after intercourse?
key_questions.looking_for: Irregular or heavier menses can accompany cysts; abnormal bleeding raises concern for other causes

key_questions.question: Have you had any vaginal discharge or pain with intercourse?
key_questions.looking_for: Purulent discharge suggests pelvic inflammatory disease; dyspareunia is common with cysts and endometriosis

key_questions.question: Have you had ovarian cysts, endometriosis, pelvic infections, or pelvic surgery before?
key_questions.looking_for: Prior cysts, endometriosis or pelvic infection increase the likelihood of cyst-related pain

key_questions.question: Have you taken fertility medications such as clomiphene, letrozole, or gonadotropins?
key_questions.looking_for: Ovulation-inducing medications increase the risk of functional and theca lutein cysts

key_questions.question: Has anyone in your family had ovarian, breast, or colon cancer?
key_questions.looking_for: A family history of breast or ovarian cancer raises concern for a hereditary cancer syndrome and malignancy

key_questions.question: Do you smoke, and how much alcohol do you drink?
key_questions.looking_for: Smoking is a weak risk factor for cysts and is relevant to overall risk assessment

key_questions.question: Have you had any unintentional weight loss, early fullness with meals, or night sweats?
key_questions.looking_for: These suggest malignancy rather than a benign cyst and require urgent evaluation

key_questions.question: Have you fainted, felt lightheaded, or had a racing heart?
key_questions.looking_for: Syncope, lightheadedness or palpitations suggest a ruptured cyst with significant bleeding

reasoning_points: Unilateral lower abdominal or pelvic pain or pressure in a woman of reproductive age
Gradual onset of mild to moderate, intermittent pain that may worsen with activity or intercourse
Associated bloating, fullness, urinary frequency, or irregular menses
No fever, no peritoneal signs, and a negative pregnancy test
Bimanual exam may reveal a palpable adnexal mass or focal adnexal tenderness on one side
Transvaginal ultrasound shows a simple cyst with a thin smooth wall, anechoic fluid, no septations, and no solid components
Pregnancy excluded before imaging or intervention
Red flags for torsion or rupture (sudden severe pain, vomiting, syncope, hemodynamic instability) are absent or appropriately evaluated

easy: Reproductive-age woman with mild unilateral pelvic pressure and bloating
Pain worse with activity or intercourse
Bimanual exam reveals a palpable adnexal mass
Transvaginal ultrasound shows a simple cyst with a thin wall and no solid components
medium: Incidental cyst found on imaging done for another reason, with minimal or no symptoms
Hemorrhagic cyst with internal echoes or a lacy pattern on ultrasound
Irregular menses with mild pelvic pain and a normal exam
Cyst in a postmenopausal woman requiring evaluation for malignancy
Overlapping symptoms with urinary tract infection or endometriosis
hard: Sudden severe unilateral pain with vomiting suggesting ovarian torsion
Ruptured cyst with tachycardia, hypotension, or falling hemoglobin
Fever and purulent discharge suggesting pelvic inflammatory disease or tubo-ovarian abscess
Complex or solid adnexal mass with ascites or elevated CA-125 suggesting ovarian cancer
Right lower quadrant pain mimicking appendicitis
Cyst discovered during pregnancy with limited imaging options
